x: High Courts are in Part VI (the States), Chapter V, Articles 214–231. The Supreme Court is in Part V, Chapter IV, Articles 124–147.
t: Discriminate the Supreme Court's Articles (124–147) from the High Courts' (214–231).

x: The Indian High Courts Act, 1861 led to the first three High Courts, at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras, in 1862. Agra came in 1866 and moved to Allahabad in 1869.
t: Recall the three presidency High Courts of 1862.

x: The three presidency High Courts came first (1862), then the North-Western Provinces High Court at Agra (1866), which moved to Allahabad (1869). The order is C, A, B.
t: Recall the years 1862, 1866 and 1869.

x: Under Article 216, the President fixes the number of judges of each High Court. For the Supreme Court, Parliament fixes the number by law (Article 124(1)).
t: Discriminate who fixes the number of judges in each court.

x: Article 215 makes High Courts Courts of Record, 216 sets their composition, 222 provides transfer, and 231 a common High Court. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall Articles 215, 216, 222 and 231.

x: A is true: the President appoints High Court judges by warrant under Article 217. B is false because the Governor administers their oath under Article 219.
t: Discriminate who appoints a judge from who swears them in.

x: A High Court judge retires at 62, takes the oath before the Governor, and resigns to the President, and the Court of Record provision is Article 215. The answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
t: Discriminate who swears a judge in from whom they resign to.

x: Option B is incorrect: a High Court judge's salary is charged on the State's fund, but the pension on the Consolidated Fund of India.
t: Discriminate High Court judges' salary (State) from their pension (Union).

x: I and II are correct: Article 220 limits practice after retirement and 223 covers the Acting Chief Justice. III is false because Article 227 is superintendence; the writ power is in Article 226.
t: Discriminate Article 226 (writs) from Article 227 (superintendence).

x: I, II and III are correct: a High Court judge must be a citizen with 10 years in judicial office or 10 years as a High Court advocate. IV is false because the distinguished-jurist route exists only for the Supreme Court.
t: Recall the extra route to the Supreme Court.

x: Article 218 applies the Supreme Court's removal rules, 224/224A cover additional, acting and retired judges, 226 writs, and 230 extension to Union Territories. The answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall Articles 218, 224, 226 and 230.

x: Option B is incorrect: under Article 227(4), superintendence does not cover courts and tribunals set up under Armed Forces laws. It does cover all other courts and tribunals in the High Court's territory, judicially and administratively.
t: Recall the Armed Forces exception in Article 227.

x: Both are true: under Article 231, Parliament can set up one High Court for two or more States and Union Territories, and Article 230 lets it extend a High Court's jurisdiction to a Union Territory.
t: Recall Articles 230 and 231.

x: Bombay covers Maharashtra, Goa, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu. Calcutta covers West Bengal and the Andamans, Kerala covers Lakshadweep, and Madras covers Puducherry. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Pair each island or coastal UT with its High Court.

x: Two are correct: Punjab and Haryana (with Chandigarh) and Gauhati (Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram, Arunachal). Puducherry and Lakshadweep are swapped: Kerala covers Lakshadweep and Madras covers Puducherry.
t: Pair each island or coastal UT with its High Court.

x: Under Article 220, a retired permanent High Court judge can plead only before the Supreme Court and other High Courts, not the one where they served.
t: Discriminate the bars on retired Supreme Court and High Court judges.

x: Option B is incorrect: High Courts have no general advisory jurisdiction. Only the Supreme Court gives advisory opinions, under Article 143. Both are Courts of Record (Articles 215 and 129).
t: Recall that only the Supreme Court has advisory jurisdiction.

x: Article 214 says there shall be a High Court for each State. Article 231 allows a common one for two or more States.
t: Recall Article 214.

x: As Courts of Record under Article 215, High Courts' records count as evidence, and they can punish contempt of themselves.
t: Recall what being a Court of Record means.

x: Both are true: other High Court judges are appointed after consulting the CJI, the Governor and the High Court's Chief Justice, which is wider than the consultation for the Chief Justice (CJI and Governor only). R explains A.
t: Compare whom the President consults for the Chief Justice and for other judges.

x: Both are true: High Courts' writ power under Article 226 is discretionary, and Article 32 is a fundamental right. A fact about Article 32 cannot explain Article 226, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether a fact about Article 32 explains Article 226.

x: Article 215 makes High Courts Courts of Record, 221 covers salaries and pensions, 223 the Acting Chief Justice, and 227 superintendence. The answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.
t: Recall Articles 215, 221, 223 and 227.

x: For a High Court Chief Justice, the President consults the CJI and Governor. For other judges, also the High Court's Chief Justice. Judges need citizenship and 10 years' experience, and there is no jurist route. The answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Compare whom the President consults for the Chief Justice and for other judges.

x: Article 224 covers additional and acting judges, 224A retired judges sitting, 227 superintendence, and 230 extension to Union Territories. The answer is a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
t: Recall Articles 224, 224A, 227 and 230.

x: I and II are correct: Article 215 makes High Courts Courts of Record with contempt powers. III is false because the Acting Chief Justice is under Article 223.
t: Recall Articles 215 and 223.

x: I, II and III are correct: under Article 227, superintendence is both administrative and judicial and covers the whole territory. IV is false because Armed Forces courts and tribunals are excluded.
t: Recall the Armed Forces exception in Article 227.

x: Both are true: High Court judges' salaries are charged on the State's fund and their pensions on the Consolidated Fund of India.
t: Discriminate High Court judges' salary (State) from their pension (Union).

x: Both are true: High Courts have no general advisory jurisdiction, while the Supreme Court has one under Article 143.
t: Recall that only the Supreme Court has advisory jurisdiction.

x: Article 226 lets High Courts issue writs for fundamental rights and 'for any other purpose'. Article 32 is limited to fundamental rights.
t: Discriminate Article 32 (fundamental rights only) from Article 226 (other rights too).

x: The High Court for the North-Western Provinces was set up at Agra in 1866 and moved to Allahabad in 1869.
t: Discriminate the 1866 setting-up from the 1869 move.

x: Both are true: Article 216 lets the President fix a High Court's strength, while Article 124(1) lets Parliament fix the Supreme Court's by law. R explains the difference in A.
t: Discriminate who fixes the number of judges in each court.

x: Supreme Court judges are appointed by warrant under Article 124 and resign to the President. Its writ power is Article 32 and its advisory power Article 143. The answer is a-iv, b-ii, c-i, d-iii.
t: Recall Articles 124, 32 and 143.

x: Three are correct: Supreme Court judges retire at 65, its writ power is Article 32, and its advisory power Article 143. Statement IV is false because its Court of Record Article is 129; 215 is for High Courts.
t: Pair Article 129 (Supreme Court) with Article 215 (High Courts).

x: High Courts' writ power is wider because Article 226 covers fundamental rights and other legal rights, while Article 32 covers only fundamental rights.
t: Discriminate Article 32 (fundamental rights only) from Article 226 (other rights too).

x: I and II are correct: the President consults the CJI and Governor for a High Court Chief Justice, and also the High Court's Chief Justice for other judges. III is false because the President appoints, not the Governor.
t: Discriminate who appoints from who is consulted.

x: Article 219 covers the oath, 217(1)(a) resignation, 217(1)(b) with 124(4) removal, and 220 practice after retirement. The answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the clauses of Article 217.

x: Like a Supreme Court judge, a High Court judge is removed by the President only after each House passes an address by special majority for proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
t: Recall that both courts' judges are removed the same way.

x: Under Article 124(6), the President administers the oath to Supreme Court judges. The Governor does it for High Court judges.
t: Discriminate who swears in each court's judges.

x: A Supreme Court judge's salary and pension are both charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. Option C describes a High Court judge.
t: Discriminate the Supreme Court (both Union) from the High Courts (salary from the State).

x: Tribunals are in Part XIV-A, Articles 323-A and 323-B. Part XIV covers services and Part XI Centre-State relations.
t: Discriminate Part XIV (services) from Part XIV-A (tribunals).

x: The 42nd Amendment, 1976, inserted Part XIV-A on tribunals, following the Swaran Singh Committee.
t: Recall the 42nd Amendment's additions.

x: The Swaran Singh Committee (1976) recommended the tribunals in Part XIV-A. The Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions dealt with Centre-State relations.
t: Discriminate the Swaran Singh Committee from the Centre-State commissions.

x: Both are true: tribunals are quasi-judicial bodies set up to reduce the courts' backlog and bring specialist expertise.
t: Recall why tribunals were created.

x: Both are true: in L. Chandra Kumar (1997), the Supreme Court held that judicial review by High Courts (Articles 226/227) and the Supreme Court (Article 32) is part of the basic structure. R names the ruling behind A.
t: Recall the 1997 L. Chandra Kumar ruling.

x: Option B is incorrect: L. Chandra Kumar struck down the clauses excluding the courts, so tribunal decisions go first to a High Court Division Bench, then to the Supreme Court.
t: Recall the route of appeal after L. Chandra Kumar.

x: Article 323-A covers administrative tribunals, 323-B tribunals for other matters, 226/227 High Court review, and 32 Supreme Court review. The answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Discriminate Article 323-A (service matters) from 323-B (other matters).

x: Option B is incorrect: only Parliament can set up tribunals under Article 323-A. That Article covers only public service matters (recruitment and conditions of service).
t: Discriminate who can set up tribunals under 323-A and 323-B.

x: Part IX covers Panchayats, IX-A Municipalities, IX-B co-operative societies, and XIV services. The answer is a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the order of Parts IX, IX-A and IX-B.

x: The Central Administrative Tribunal was set up in 1985 under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985.
t: Recall the year of the CAT.

x: A is true: the CAT has original jurisdiction over Union civil servants' service matters. B is false because appeals go first to a High Court Division Bench, not straight to the Supreme Court.
t: Recall the route of appeal from the CAT.

x: TDSAT was set up by the TRAI (Amendment) Act, 2000, which amended the original TRAI Act of 1997.
t: Discriminate the 1997 TRAI Act from the 2000 amendment.

x: I, II and III are correct: TDSAT decides telecom, broadcasting and airport tariff disputes. IV is false because its cyber appellate orders go to the High Court.
t: Discriminate TDSAT's appeal routes.

x: The CAT hears Union service matters, TDSAT telecom and tariff disputes, the NGT environmental disputes, and IMDT tribunals decided who was an illegal migrant. The answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
t: Match each tribunal to its subject.

x: The National Green Tribunal is a statutory body set up under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010.
t: Recall the NGT's Act and year.

x: Both are true: the NGT follows the principles of natural justice rather than the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. R explains A.
t: Ask whether following natural justice explains not being bound by the CPC.

x: Appeals against NGT orders go straight to the Supreme Court, within 90 days.
t: Recall the NGT's 90-day appeal period.

x: Option C is incorrect: the IMDT Act (1983) was struck down in Sarbananda Sonowal (2005) for violating Article 355, the Union's duty to protect States against external aggression.
t: Recall the 2005 Sarbananda Sonowal ruling.

x: The CAT came first (1985), then L. Chandra Kumar (1997), TDSAT (2000) and the NGT (2010). The order is A, B, C, D.
t: Recall the years 1985, 1997, 2000 and 2010.

x: All four are subjects under Article 323-B: taxation, foreign exchange, industrial disputes, and elections to Parliament and State Legislatures. Land reforms, property ceilings and foodstuffs are also listed.
t: Recall the subjects of Article 323-B.

x: Both are true: Article 227(4) keeps Armed Forces courts and tribunals out of High Court superintendence, which the Armed Forces Tribunal Act, 2007 reflects. R explains A.
t: Recall the Armed Forces exception in Article 227.

x: Since L. Chandra Kumar, a decision of the CAT or similar tribunals goes to a Division Bench of the High Court before the Supreme Court.
t: Recall the route of appeal after L. Chandra Kumar.

x: Both are true: only Parliament can set up tribunals under Article 323-A. Under 323-B, both Parliament and State Legislatures can, within their own legislative fields.
t: Discriminate who can set up tribunals under 323-A and 323-B.

x: Article 323-A covers public service matters and only Parliament can act under it. Article 323-B covers other listed subjects and both Parliament and States can act. The answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Discriminate who can set up tribunals under 323-A and 323-B.

x: The CAT was set up under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985, the law made under Article 323-A.
t: Recall the Act behind the CAT.

x: Option B is incorrect: the CAT comes under Article 323-A (service matters), not 323-B. It was set up by the 1985 Act and hears Union service matters.
t: Discriminate Article 323-A (service matters) from 323-B (other matters).

x: Both are true: TDSAT's cyber appellate orders go to the High Court, while telecom, broadcasting and tariff appeals go straight to the Supreme Court on substantial questions of law.
t: Discriminate TDSAT's appeal routes.

x: I, II and III are correct: Part IX covers Panchayats, IX-A Municipalities and IX-B co-operatives. IV is false because Part XIV-A covers tribunals; services are in Part XIV.
t: Discriminate Part XIV (services) from Part XIV-A (tribunals).

x: Both are true: Article 323-A provides one Central Administrative Tribunal plus State (or joint) tribunals, and Article 323-B allows a hierarchy of tribunals.
t: Discriminate the structures under 323-A and 323-B.

x: Both are true: Part XI deals with Union-State relations, and Part X with Scheduled and Tribal Areas.
t: Recall the subjects of Parts X and XI.
